output:
Read before deploy, not after

Four constraints that break this service quietly

Each one was found in production rather than anticipated in design. Three of them fail without an error. Budget fifteen minutes now instead of an afternoon later.

The short version

  1. One replica. Not two. Replay protection doesn't degrade under scaling — it stops working.
  2. Long polls die at ~100s behind Cloudflare. Keep MAX_AWAIT_MS under your proxy's ceiling.
  3. Link agents to /mcp, never /mcp.js. A CDN may cache by extension no matter what headers you send.
  4. Participant links are capabilities, not identities. This is not an audit trail. Don't promise one.

1.Run exactly one replica

Hard constraint — do not change alone

The replay-protection nonce store is in memory (src/adapters/crypto/nonces.ts). Every signed request carries a nonce that is accepted once, and that single-use rule is what stops a captured request being replayed inside its five-minute freshness window.

Why this is the important one

With two replicas, a nonce burned on one is unknown to the other. A replayed request routed to the second replica succeeds. Replay protection does not degrade under horizontal scaling; it stops working.

The Deployment therefore pins replicas: 1 with a Recreate strategy. That is the single most important operational constraint in this service.

Scaling out is possible. It means moving the nonce store to Postgres or Redis first. The moment someone edits replicas, that is the change that has to land with it — same commit, same review.

2.Long polls die at about 100 seconds behind Cloudflare

Check this against your own proxy

Cloudflare gives an origin roughly 100 seconds to respond before it answers 524 on its own account.

Measured through the tunnel

A 150-second poll died at 125 seconds with HTTP 524 and no body. Not a slow response — no response, and no way for the caller to distinguish a dead wait from an empty one.

Holding a connection past that ceiling does not make the caller wait longer. It makes the wait fail. So MAX_AWAIT_MS defaults to 90 seconds: every poll returns inside the window, and one that exhausts its budget comes back with timedOut: true plus whatever has arrived so far. A timeout is a legitimate outcome here, not an error. The MCP client loops shorter polls, so a caller asking for five minutes still gets five minutes.

Behind a different proxy, find its timeout and set MAX_AWAIT_MS below it. Whatever sits in front of this service decides the real ceiling; the service only decides whether it respects it.

3.A CDN may cache by file extension regardless of what you send

Silent failure — verify at the edge

/mcp.js was served with cache-control: no-store and came back from the edge with cf-cache-status: HIT and an injected max-age=14400. Cloudflare caches .js by default, by extension, whatever the origin intended.

What that cost

For four hours after every deploy, agents installed the previous client. Nothing errored. Everything worked — one deploy behind.

The fix is in the path, not in the headers. The canonical URL for the MCP client is /mcp, with no extension. /mcp.js remains as an alias for anyone who saved the old URL, but nothing new should point at it.

If you put any CDN in front of this, check what it caches by default. Origin headers are a request, not an instruction.

4.Participant links are capabilities

Set expectations before rollout

Anyone holding a participant link can answer as that participant. A forwarded link is a forwarded identity.

This is deliberate, and it is the reason the product works at all: participants need no account, no email verification, and no Claude access. Attribution is whichever link was used — which costs nothing and is honest about what it is.

Say this out loud to your team

It is not an audit trail. Do not deploy this expecting one. If responses ever need to be contested, that is the moment to add verified identity — and that is a change to this service, not a configuration option waiting to be switched on.

What you do control is the window:

  • LINK_TTL_HOURS bounds how long a link stays answerable. Expiry is checked in the query that resolves a token, not after it.
  • The schema carries revoked_at and honours it on every resolve — but nothing exposes revocation over HTTP yet. Killing one link today is an update against participant_links.

Decide now who on your team can run that update at 2am, and make sure they know it's the only lever.

Pre-deploy checklist

  • replicas: 1 and strategy Recreate confirmed in the Deployment manifest.
  • A note on the Deployment (or in review rules) that changing replicas requires an external nonce store first.
  • Your proxy's response timeout identified, and MAX_AWAIT_MS set comfortably below it.
  • Callers handle timedOut: true as a normal outcome, not an error path.
  • Every install instruction, doc and bookmark points at /mcp, not /mcp.js.
  • After the first deploy: fetch the client through the edge and confirm you get the new build, not a cached one.
  • LINK_TTL_HOURS chosen deliberately for how your team actually shares links.
  • Someone with database access knows how to revoke a link by hand, and the team knows links are shareable identities.
Adapted from docs/SELF-HOSTING.md — “Constraints that are measured, not theoretical.” Every figure here was observed in production, not estimated.
